cur:objects2-shemokmedi-crucifixion-quat.summary: On a small quatrefoil of gold, about 8 cm high, the crucified Christ hangs on a dark cross beneath the inscription tablet, flanked by the Virgin and Saint John and by two angels above; Greek-letter inscriptions surround the scene. The brilliant colours of the enamel against the gold ground make the image glow like a jewel. It came from the monastery of Shemokmedi in western Georgia, whose treasury preserved many Georgian and Byzantine precious objects.
facts: The Commons record gives its size as 8 × 7.2 cm and describes it as cellular (cloisonné) enamel on a golden ground.
The Shemokmedi treasury, in Guria, also held the Transfiguration icon brought from Zarzma monastery in the 16th century.
cur:objects2-shemokmedi-crucifixion-quat.notes: Date and attribution follow the Commons file description; I could not consult the museum catalogue.

Q2528741.summary: Velázquez sets a life-size Christ against a plain greenish-dark background, alone and utterly still, with no mourners, landscape or drama to distract from contemplation. The body is serenely classical, lit softly from the left; the head has fallen forward and a curtain of long hair hides more than half of the face. Its quiet restraint has made it one of the most beloved and meditated-upon images of the Crucifixion in Spain.
facts: Christ is fixed with four nails, his feet side by side on a small footrest, following the recommendation of Velázquez's teacher and father-in-law, the painter and theorist Francisco Pacheco.

It was painted for the convent of Benedictine nuns of San Plácido in Madrid, probably given by the convent's founder Jerónimo de Villanueva; it later belonged to Manuel Godoy and entered the Prado in 1829.
The philosopher Miguel de Unamuno devoted a long poem, El Cristo de Velázquez (1920), to meditating on this painting.
A later legend claimed that King Philip IV commissioned the painting in atonement for an affair with a nun of San Plácido; historians regard the story as unfounded.
